newsitem.title: INDIA: Bangladesh PM offers prayers at start of India trip.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM offers prayers at start of India trip.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina arrived in India on Tuesday at the start of a three-day visit considered a crucial test of her six-month old leadership.

Hasina arrived in the Indian capital and immediately set off on a private visit to the western state of Rajasthan where she offered prayers at the tomb of Moslem saint Khwaja Moinuddin Chisti at Ajmer, an Indian government spokesman said.
Hasina was received by the head priest of the shrine and presented with a purple "chador", officials in the Rajasthan capital Jaipur said.
She was scheduled to stay overnight at Jaipur and leave for Delhi on Wednesday, they said.

The official leg of her trip was to begin in New Delhi on Wednesday when she was scheduled to meet Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and the Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral after a reception at the presidential palace.
Hasina was accompanied by Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad and Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak.
At the top of Hasina's agenda will be the issue of tapping water from the Ganges, which flows through India into Bangladesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
The decades-old water dispute, which worsened after India built its Farakka Barrage in 1974 restricting the Ganges flow, has often soured relations between the two neighbours.
Dhaka says the barrage, 18 km (11 miles) from Bangladesh's northern border, deprives Bangladesh of its fair share of water and leaves 40 million people exposed to gradual desertification.

Political opponents deride Hasina, who assumed power in June after elections, as a "stooge of India" because her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, signed a 25-year friendship treaty with India.

Although Hasina has said the treaty will not be renewed when it expires next March, her critics still brand her "too pro-Indian", a tag they have long tried to use keep her and her Awami League out of power.
Ganges water sharing is considered the foremost issue to be tackled before next dry season begins at end of 1996.

Dhaka said a draft water-sharing agreement was prepared during a recent visit to Bangladesh by Jyoti Basu, the powerful communist chief minister of India's West Bengal state, which also needs hefty volumes of Ganges water for its Calcutta port.
Officials said barring any last-minute hitches, Hasina and Deve Gowda were expected to sign the agreement on Thursday. They were tight-lipped, however, about details of the accord.
The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party, headed by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, has demanded the accord be heard in parliament before being accepted.
